compare_blocks.body:
Align the conditions first: the same roadmap draft, the same attendees, the same three-year horizon and budget ceiling. If one is the decision maker and the other only consulted, role will swamp both columns.

| --- | --- | --- | --- |

compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
In a fictional roadmap review, either participant can ask about near-term delivery or what customers might need in three years. The meeting’s purpose and each person’s responsibilities help explain the questions they ask.

The shared N concerns patterns and possibilities. The shared J concerns a preference for clear outward arrangements. Neither preference tells you which deadline someone will propose or how much detail they will check.

The difference sits in two preferences. E/I is where attention lands: more often on what others think, who has not been asked yet, which party in the room has not declared a position — or more often on whether that internal chain of reasoning has been finished. T/F is the basis for judgement: more often asking whether the standard applies consistently and which year the cost lands in, or more often asking what this means for the people involved and whose commitment gets broken. Both have to be read; neither can be replaced by a phrase about whose plan is harder.

### ENFJ and INTJ: one three-year roadmap, two acceptable bases

In a fictional review, two colleagues have the same three-year roadmap, budget and staffing options. They must weigh fixing existing problems against building a new product channel.

Either reviewer can consider the commitments already made to customers and the burden each option would place on teams. Either can also compare both options against the same cost, capacity and risk criteria. These are two ways to weigh the same evidence, illustrating T/F.

A proposal may be difficult to carry out if it overlooks the people responsible for it. A popular proposal may still depend on an assumption the evidence cannot support. Both issues can be recorded in the same decision.

What shows in the meeting is not who speaks first but which reason each treats as enough. Question order is shaped by the agenda, the rank in the room and who did the homework beforehand, and cannot be used to assign a type. Conditions also rewrite behaviour: with the direction clear and only sponsorship missing, an INTJ may also go and persuade key people one by one; with the direction still fuzzy and resources already contested, an ENFJ may also demand the assumptions be written before any division of work. Duty, authority, deadline and available information all take part, and one meeting cannot settle a person.

### ENFJ and INTJ: why Ni and Se are shared while both judging functions change

In the four-function notation used here, ENFJ is Fe–Ni–Se–Ti and INTJ is Ni–Te–Fi–Se. What is shared is the two perceiving processes: Ni second in ENFJ and first in INTJ, Se third in ENFJ and fourth in INTJ. The shared processes change positions, and the two full stacks are not reversals of each other.

The two judging seats change family, not attitude. Fe and Te both face outward, one Feeling and one Thinking; Ti and Fi both face inward, likewise split. So the correspondence is Fe against Te and Ti against Fi: the attitude stays and what changes is whether judgement looks at people or at criteria.

Both types have J, so type dynamics identifies their outward process as judging. For extraverted ENFJ, that process is dominant Fe. For introverted INTJ, it is auxiliary Te, while the inward-facing Ni is dominant. The positions describe the model and do not predict who will speak first.

The attitude of the third process (Se in ENFJ, Fi in INTJ) is labelled inconsistently; this page takes the common writing, and the disagreement does not change the first two positions or explain how early someone acts. Position describes emphasis only and is not used to infer who does what first, who is better at which segment, or whether two people get along. compare_blocks.body:
When the two work together, the easiest split is not by type but by who holds the information and who holds outward authority: whoever writes the premises and the give-ups need not be the INTJ, and whoever confirms section by section with key people need not be the ENFJ.

### ENFJ and INTJ: a three-year roadmap review, with technical debt and new business after the same team

(Fictional scene) The company is building a three-year roadmap. Engineering says the technical debt has to be paid; the business side says the new channel has to be built; both need the same six-person team. The review has run two hours and the deck is still arguing at page ten.

In this fictional review, either colleague can ask engineering and sales which commitments are at risk. Either can also test how both options hold up against the same staffing and capacity assumptions. The decision record can include both the effects on stakeholders and the criteria used to choose.

The costs differ: translating the conflict repeatedly into a sentence everyone can accept tends to produce a schedule while the substantive conflict moves to next year; judging too hard can leave nobody willing to supply information. The workable pairing has nothing to do with type: whoever knows the assumption chain best writes one page of premises and give-ups, whoever holds the relationships best takes it to the two leads separately, converts "giving up" into acceptable compensation, and brings it back to the room.

To check the map, look at whether the trade-offs were recorded, not at who persuaded whom. Read the internal decision note and confirm whether the key trade-offs, their grounds and the open items are written; if not, ask whether they are undecided or recorded somewhere else. Four things to do listed on their own may only be this version for external use, and cannot be taken as evidence that consensus overrode the trade-off. Counterexamples belong here too: with the direction set and only sponsorship missing, an INTJ will book people one by one; with the assumptions unwritten, an ENFJ will ask for a page of premises first.

Two notes each before the meeting also work: one line for what must be true in three years, one for what has to be done this year. Put the four side by side afterwards and check first whether the two "must be true" statements can hold at once, then whether they point at conflicting resource choices; if they can hold, discuss scheduling, and if not, discuss direction first. That checks the decision, not the type.

### ENFJ and INTJ: one page for senior management, and what to cut

(Fictional scene) The roadmap has to become one page for the board and one page for clients, from a twelve-page draft.

Working from the same draft, either reviewer can ask what the board needs to decide and what clients need to know. A board brief can explain the options and trade-offs. A client update can describe the confirmed commitments and timing.

Each version should be accurate about what has been decided. A shorter client update can omit internal options if it still gives a clear account of the service commitments. What is included does not show who persuaded whom.

### ENFJ and INTJ: a friend of twelve years has to tell his parents about a debt

(Fictional scene) Move the camera somewhere no salary is involved, and the same split in judgement appears. A friend of twelve years has closed his shop, owes a hundred and eighty thousand, and his parents do not know.

In this fictional scene, one approach asks how he and his parents usually talk and how his mother's health is, then offers to go back with him and sit alongside to help him finish the sentences. The other breaks the debt down: which payments are pressing, at what interest, how many months to clear it, and what the family can realistically do once told. Either type can combine both; which step gets taken depends on the division of work, authority and the information available.

In the fictional conversation, either friend can ask what support is wanted before offering to attend or help organize information. Considering how the conversation will affect the family is an example of a Feeling consideration. Applying the same criteria to the information is an example of a Thinking consideration. Either person can use both.

Someone who asks about the family may also want to see the relevant documents. Someone who asks for the documents may also want to understand how the friend feels. Those questions do not identify a type.

One check: before meeting the parents, each writes one sentence on what this conversation has to achieve — one sentence only. If the two differ, settle that sentence first instead of walking through the door.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
Reading INTJ as not caring about people is the most common misreading of this pair. Rejecting a proposal in a meeting usually means the path was calculated and does not work, not that the person proposing it does not matter; the same person may remember better than anyone whether the other can absorb the news, and simply not write that layer into the conclusion.

An ENFJ can have a firm view, and an INTJ can decide to hold back an opinion. How much someone says in one meeting does not establish what they believe.

The third misread turns E/I into who expresses themselves better or works a room better. Both can explain a three-year plan clearly: fluency in speaking comes from practice and setting, and choosing whom to tell comes from strategy and duty — neither distinguishes E/I. E/I describes whether attention and energy turn outward or inward more often: someone who says little all meeting may have had their attention on other people the whole time.

body: In a fictional roadmap review, either participant can ask about near-term delivery or what customers might need in three years. The meeting’s purpose and each person’s responsibilities help explain the questions they ask.

The shared N concerns patterns and possibilities. The shared J concerns a preference for clear outward arrangements. Neither preference tells you which deadline someone will propose or how much detail they will check.

The difference sits in two preferences. E/I is where attention lands: more often on what others think, who has not been asked yet, which party in the room has not declared a position — or more often on whether that internal chain of reasoning has been finished. T/F is the basis for judgement: more often asking whether the standard applies consistently and which year the cost lands in, or more often asking what this means for the people involved and whose commitment gets broken. Both have to be read; neither can be replaced by a phrase about whose plan is harder.
### ENFJ and INTJ: one three-year roadmap, two acceptable bases
In a fictional review, two colleagues have the same three-year roadmap, budget and staffing options. They must weigh fixing existing problems against building a new product channel.

Either reviewer can consider the commitments already made to customers and the burden each option would place on teams. Either can also compare both options against the same cost, capacity and risk criteria. These are two ways to weigh the same evidence, illustrating T/F.

A proposal may be difficult to carry out if it overlooks the people responsible for it. A popular proposal may still depend on an assumption the evidence cannot support. Both issues can be recorded in the same decision.

What shows in the meeting is not who speaks first but which reason each treats as enough. Question order is shaped by the agenda, the rank in the room and who did the homework beforehand, and cannot be used to assign a type. Conditions also rewrite behaviour: with the direction clear and only sponsorship missing, an INTJ may also go and persuade key people one by one; with the direction still fuzzy and resources already contested, an ENFJ may also demand the assumptions be written before any division of work. Duty, authority, deadline and available information all take part, and one meeting cannot settle a person.
### ENFJ and INTJ: why Ni and Se are shared while both judging functions change

In the four-function notation used here, ENFJ is Fe–Ni–Se–Ti and INTJ is Ni–Te–Fi–Se. What is shared is the two perceiving processes: Ni second in ENFJ and first in INTJ, Se third in ENFJ and fourth in INTJ. The shared processes change positions, and the two full stacks are not reversals of each other.

The two judging seats change family, not attitude. Fe and Te both face outward, one Feeling and one Thinking; Ti and Fi both face inward, likewise split. So the correspondence is Fe against Te and Ti against Fi: the attitude stays and what changes is whether judgement looks at people or at criteria.

Both types have J, so type dynamics identifies their outward process as judging. For extraverted ENFJ, that process is dominant Fe. For introverted INTJ, it is auxiliary Te, while the inward-facing Ni is dominant. The positions describe the model and do not predict who will speak first.

The attitude of the third process (Se in ENFJ, Fi in INTJ) is labelled inconsistently; this page takes the common writing, and the disagreement does not change the first two positions or explain how early someone acts. Position describes emphasis only and is not used to infer who does what first, who is better at which segment, or whether two people get along. Base descriptions sit on the [ENFJ profile](/en/personality/enfj) and the [INTJ profile](/en/personality/intj).

body: When the two work together, the easiest split is not by type but by who holds the information and who holds outward authority: whoever writes the premises and the give-ups need not be the INTJ, and whoever confirms section by section with key people need not be the ENFJ.
### ENFJ and INTJ: a three-year roadmap review, with technical debt and new business after the same team

(Fictional scene) The company is building a three-year roadmap. Engineering says the technical debt has to be paid; the business side says the new channel has to be built; both need the same six-person team. The review has run two hours and the deck is still arguing at page ten.

In this fictional review, either colleague can ask engineering and sales which commitments are at risk. Either can also test how both options hold up against the same staffing and capacity assumptions. The decision record can include both the effects on stakeholders and the criteria used to choose.

The costs differ: translating the conflict repeatedly into a sentence everyone can accept tends to produce a schedule while the substantive conflict moves to next year; judging too hard can leave nobody willing to supply information. The workable pairing has nothing to do with type: whoever knows the assumption chain best writes one page of premises and give-ups, whoever holds the relationships best takes it to the two leads separately, converts "giving up" into acceptable compensation, and brings it back to the room.

To check the map, look at whether the trade-offs were recorded, not at who persuaded whom. Read the internal decision note and confirm whether the key trade-offs, their grounds and the open items are written; if not, ask whether they are undecided or recorded somewhere else. Four things to do listed on their own may only be this version for external use, and cannot be taken as evidence that consensus overrode the trade-off. Counterexamples belong here too: with the direction set and only sponsorship missing, an INTJ will book people one by one; with the assumptions unwritten, an ENFJ will ask for a page of premises first.

Two notes each before the meeting also work: one line for what must be true in three years, one for what has to be done this year. Put the four side by side afterwards and check first whether the two "must be true" statements can hold at once, then whether they point at conflicting resource choices; if they can hold, discuss scheduling, and if not, discuss direction first. That checks the decision, not the type.
### ENFJ and INTJ: one page for senior management, and what to cut
(Fictional scene) The roadmap has to become one page for the board and one page for clients, from a twelve-page draft.

Working from the same draft, either reviewer can ask what the board needs to decide and what clients need to know. A board brief can explain the options and trade-offs. A client update can describe the confirmed commitments and timing.

Each version should be accurate about what has been decided. A shorter client update can omit internal options if it still gives a clear account of the service commitments. What is included does not show who persuaded whom.
### ENFJ and INTJ: a friend of twelve years has to tell his parents about a debt

(Fictional scene) Move the camera somewhere no salary is involved, and the same split in judgement appears. A friend of twelve years has closed his shop, owes a hundred and eighty thousand, and his parents do not know.

In this fictional scene, one approach asks how he and his parents usually talk and how his mother's health is, then offers to go back with him and sit alongside to help him finish the sentences. The other breaks the debt down: which payments are pressing, at what interest, how many months to clear it, and what the family can realistically do once told. Either type can combine both; which step gets taken depends on the division of work, authority and the information available.

In the fictional conversation, either friend can ask what support is wanted before offering to attend or help organize information. Considering how the conversation will affect the family is an example of a Feeling consideration. Applying the same criteria to the information is an example of a Thinking consideration. Either person can use both.

Someone who asks about the family may also want to see the relevant documents. Someone who asks for the documents may also want to understand how the friend feels. Those questions do not identify a type.

One check: before meeting the parents, each writes one sentence on what this conversation has to achieve — one sentence only. If the two differ, settle that sentence first instead of walking through the door.

body: Reading INTJ as not caring about people is the most common misreading of this pair. Rejecting a proposal in a meeting usually means the path was calculated and does not work, not that the person proposing it does not matter; the same person may remember better than anyone whether the other can absorb the news, and simply not write that layer into the conclusion.
An ENFJ can have a firm view, and an INTJ can decide to hold back an opinion. How much someone says in one meeting does not establish what they believe.

The third misread turns E/I into who expresses themselves better or works a room better. Both can explain a three-year plan clearly: fluency in speaking comes from practice and setting, and choosing whom to tell comes from strategy and duty — neither distinguishes E/I. E/I describes whether attention and energy turn outward or inward more often: someone who says little all meeting may have had their attention on other people the whole time.

The difference sits in two preferences. E/I is where attention lands: more often on what others think, who has not been asked yet, which party in the room has not declared a position — or more often on whether that internal chain of reasoning has been finished. T/F is the basis for judgement: more often asking whether the standard applies consistently and which year the cost lands in, or more often asking what this means for the people involved and whose commitment gets broken. Both have to be read; neither can be replaced by a phrase about whose plan is harder.

### ENFJ and INTJ: one three-year roadmap, two acceptable bases

In a fictional review, two colleagues have the same three-year roadmap, budget and staffing options. They must weigh fixing existing problems against building a new product channel.

Either reviewer can consider the commitments already made to customers and the burden each option would place on teams. Either can also compare both options against the same cost, capacity and risk criteria. These are two ways to weigh the same evidence, illustrating T/F.

A proposal may be difficult to carry out if it overlooks the people responsible for it. A popular proposal may still depend on an assumption the evidence cannot support. Both issues can be recorded in the same decision.

What shows in the meeting is not who speaks first but which reason each treats as enough. Question order is shaped by the agenda, the rank in the room and who did the homework beforehand, and cannot be used to assign a type. Conditions also rewrite behaviour: with the direction clear and only sponsorship missing, an INTJ may also go and persuade key people one by one; with the direction still fuzzy and resources already contested, an ENFJ may also demand the assumptions be written before any division of work. Duty, authority, deadline and available information all take part, and one meeting cannot settle a person.

### ENFJ and INTJ: why Ni and Se are shared while both judging functions change

In the four-function notation used here, ENFJ is Fe–Ni–Se–Ti and INTJ is Ni–Te–Fi–Se. What is shared is the two perceiving processes: Ni second in ENFJ and first in INTJ, Se third in ENFJ and fourth in INTJ. The shared processes change positions, and the two full stacks are not reversals of each other.

The two judging seats change family, not attitude. Fe and Te both face outward, one Feeling and one Thinking; Ti and Fi both face inward, likewise split. So the correspondence is Fe against Te and Ti against Fi: the attitude stays and what changes is whether judgement looks at people or at criteria.

Both types have J, so type dynamics identifies their outward process as judging. For extraverted ENFJ, that process is dominant Fe. For introverted INTJ, it is auxiliary Te, while the inward-facing Ni is dominant. The positions describe the model and do not predict who will speak first.

The attitude of the third process (Se in ENFJ, Fi in INTJ) is labelled inconsistently; this page takes the common writing, and the disagreement does not change the first two positions or explain how early someone acts. Position describes emphasis only and is not used to infer who does what first, who is better at which segment, or whether two people get along. Base descriptions sit on the [ENFJ profile](/en/personality/enfj) and the [INTJ profile](/en/personality/intj).

sections.body_md:
Align the conditions first: the same roadmap draft, the same attendees, the same three-year horizon and budget ceiling. If one is the decision maker and the other only consulted, role will swamp both columns.

Both types can use both approaches; the rows state which kind of basis is more often treated as a reason, and mark the axis each row sits on.

| The same draft, the same attendees | ENFJ: evidence likely to be attended to first | INTJ: evidence likely to be attended to first | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The draft arrives | Weigh how the same draft would affect the people expected to use it | Apply the same stated criteria to the draft’s assumptions and conclusions | Standard of judgement, leaning T/F |
| Both assess the same proposal to defer technical debt | Weigh how deferral would affect customers and the teams handling incidents | Apply the same risk, cost and capacity criteria used for comparable deferrals | Decision criteria: T/F |
| A dispute in the meeting | May clarify what the same disagreement means through discussion | May clarify what the same disagreement means through private reflection | Direction of attention, leaning E/I |
| Both assess the same proposal for a new business line | Weigh how the proposal would affect the people taking on the work and those relying on existing commitments | Apply the same feasibility and evidence standards used for other proposals | Decision criteria: T/F |
| Both review the same proposed roadmap before approval | Weigh whether the plan honors the commitments made to the people it affects | Apply the same approval criteria for evidence and trade-offs used for comparable plans | Decision criteria: T/F |
| After the review | May make sense of the same feedback by talking it through with a colleague | May make sense of the same feedback by reflecting privately | Direction of attention, leaning E/I |

None of these rows is a scale of ability. An INTJ with years of cross-department coordination will also test each party's concerns first; an ENFJ just handed a project may also spend the evening revising the reasoning. Duty, information and authority all rewrite the approach, and these rows cannot be used to classify anyone.
sections.title: ENFJ and INTJ in one minute

sections.body_md:
When the two work together, the easiest split is not by type but by who holds the information and who holds outward authority: whoever writes the premises and the give-ups need not be the INTJ, and whoever confirms section by section with key people need not be the ENFJ.

### ENFJ and INTJ: a three-year roadmap review, with technical debt and new business after the same team

(Fictional scene) The company is building a three-year roadmap. Engineering says the technical debt has to be paid; the business side says the new channel has to be built; both need the same six-person team. The review has run two hours and the deck is still arguing at page ten.

In this fictional review, either colleague can ask engineering and sales which commitments are at risk. Either can also test how both options hold up against the same staffing and capacity assumptions. The decision record can include both the effects on stakeholders and the criteria used to choose.

The costs differ: translating the conflict repeatedly into a sentence everyone can accept tends to produce a schedule while the substantive conflict moves to next year; judging too hard can leave nobody willing to supply information. The workable pairing has nothing to do with type: whoever knows the assumption chain best writes one page of premises and give-ups, whoever holds the relationships best takes it to the two leads separately, converts "giving up" into acceptable compensation, and brings it back to the room.

To check the map, look at whether the trade-offs were recorded, not at who persuaded whom. Read the internal decision note and confirm whether the key trade-offs, their grounds and the open items are written; if not, ask whether they are undecided or recorded somewhere else. Four things to do listed on their own may only be this version for external use, and cannot be taken as evidence that consensus overrode the trade-off. Counterexamples belong here too: with the direction set and only sponsorship missing, an INTJ will book people one by one; with the assumptions unwritten, an ENFJ will ask for a page of premises first.

Two notes each before the meeting also work: one line for what must be true in three years, one for what has to be done this year. Put the four side by side afterwards and check first whether the two "must be true" statements can hold at once, then whether they point at conflicting resource choices; if they can hold, discuss scheduling, and if not, discuss direction first. That checks the decision, not the type.

### ENFJ and INTJ: one page for senior management, and what to cut

(Fictional scene) The roadmap has to become one page for the board and one page for clients, from a twelve-page draft.

Working from the same draft, either reviewer can ask what the board needs to decide and what clients need to know. A board brief can explain the options and trade-offs. A client update can describe the confirmed commitments and timing.

Each version should be accurate about what has been decided. A shorter client update can omit internal options if it still gives a clear account of the service commitments. What is included does not show who persuaded whom.

### ENFJ and INTJ: a friend of twelve years has to tell his parents about a debt

(Fictional scene) Move the camera somewhere no salary is involved, and the same split in judgement appears. A friend of twelve years has closed his shop, owes a hundred and eighty thousand, and his parents do not know.

In this fictional scene, one approach asks how he and his parents usually talk and how his mother's health is, then offers to go back with him and sit alongside to help him finish the sentences. The other breaks the debt down: which payments are pressing, at what interest, how many months to clear it, and what the family can realistically do once told. Either type can combine both; which step gets taken depends on the division of work, authority and the information available.

In the fictional conversation, either friend can ask what support is wanted before offering to attend or help organize information. Considering how the conversation will affect the family is an example of a Feeling consideration. Applying the same criteria to the information is an example of a Thinking consideration. Either person can use both.

Someone who asks about the family may also want to see the relevant documents. Someone who asks for the documents may also want to understand how the friend feels. Those questions do not identify a type.

One check: before meeting the parents, each writes one sentence on what this conversation has to achieve — one sentence only. If the two differ, settle that sentence first instead of walking through the door.
sections.title: ENFJ and INTJ at work and in relationships

sections.body_md:
Reading INTJ as not caring about people is the most common misreading of this pair. Rejecting a proposal in a meeting usually means the path was calculated and does not work, not that the person proposing it does not matter; the same person may remember better than anyone whether the other can absorb the news, and simply not write that layer into the conclusion.

An ENFJ can have a firm view, and an INTJ can decide to hold back an opinion. How much someone says in one meeting does not establish what they believe.

The third misread turns E/I into who expresses themselves better or works a room better. Both can explain a three-year plan clearly: fluency in speaking comes from practice and setting, and choosing whom to tell comes from strategy and duty — neither distinguishes E/I. E/I describes whether attention and energy turn outward or inward more often: someone who says little all meeting may have had their attention on other people the whole time.

When two results differ, check whether it was the same item set, the same language version and the same scoring definition, then look back at the circumstances: did you have decision authority on the project, or only offer advice. Such conditions push answers to one side, and a single score cannot establish a stable tendency. If the report gives dimension scores, see which of E/I and T/F sits closer to a boundary; near-boundary only means that measure is sensitive to changes in answering, not that two types both hold.

Put the practice where there is a real conflict: only one project can have the budget, the team has to lose one person, a promise to the client will squeeze delivery. Write three lines for each — which kind of basis was put first, whose circumstances were counted, and what your role required of you. Read together, several cases show the entry point better than one reaction. Writing order and speed are not evidence, and there is no need to answer from a different role in order to "test accurately". If two results disagree over a long period, leave the type unsettled and record the circumstances instead.
sections.title: ENFJ and INTJ: how to keep observing

items.answer:
On E/I and T/F: E/I decides whether attention and energy turn outward or inward more often, T/F decides whether judgement rests more often on impersonal consistent criteria or includes people and values.

The ENFJ side more often treats each party's demands and commitments already made as acceptable grounds; the INTJ side more often treats whether the premises hold and which year the cost lands in as grounds. Both can look three years out, and both do the other half; the difference is which kind of reason gets cited across comparable situations, not the order within one meeting.
items.question: Looking at the same plan, where does the difference land?

items.answer:
Because two letters move at once: E/I changes which way the dominant faces, T/F changes the judging family. In the writing used here, ENFJ is Fe–Ni–Se–Ti and INTJ is Ni–Te–Fi–Se, with all four processes present.

The shared Ni and Se sit in different seats: Ni second in ENFJ and first in INTJ, Se third and fourth. So it is not a swap of positions and not a reversed order. On the judging side Fe against Te and Ti against Fi: the attitude stays, the family changes; sources label the third process differently, so check the convention when versions differ.
items.question: Why are Ni and Se shared while both judging functions change?

items.answer:
Yes, but not by the order of actions and not by who speaks better.

What discriminates better is the reason: across comparable situations, do you more often cite whether the standard applies consistently and where the cost lands, or what this means for the people involved and who needs to be included. Someone who can do both is usually switching to meet the requirements of a role, and a change of role is not a change of type.
items.question: An INTJ also looks after people's feelings, an ENFJ also overturns a consensus — can they still be told apart?

items.answer:
Not a division by type; either can own every segment of a roadmap.

A roadmap contains reading the trend, writing the reasoning, building agreement and tracking delivery. Take the same fictional roadmap and write both a list of give-ups and a sequence for key-person communication, and see which segment you would rather start from — that is practice, not a judgement of who does it better, and not a ranking of ability. Actual division follows professional experience, information held and authority; the gap between two people of the same type in different posts is often wider than the gap between types.
items.question: Which is better suited to strategy or roadmaps?

items.answer:
Usually on whether a document counts as final: one holds that key people nodding settles it, the other that it is not settled until the premises and give-ups are written.

A workable agreement splits the document into two layers: a judgement layer with premises, trade-offs and open items, and a commitment layer with what is said to clients and the team, both signed before it is final. Who closes which layer follows who holds the information and who has outward authority at the time, not type. Writing the agreement down is more useful than arguing about who is more rigorous.
items.question: Working on a project together, where do they most often jam?

items.answer:
Keep both for now, and confirm first whether it was the same item set, the same language version and the same scoring definition.

If the report gives dimension scores, see whether E/I and T/F sit near a boundary; near-boundary only means those two are sensitive to changes in answering. Look back at whether you had decision authority and whether you were referring to work or to things at home, and record that. Do not settle the result by writing speed, by which question came first, or by how many times each appeared, and do not retest from a deliberately different role; if two results disagree over a long period, leave the type unsettled.
